entries.objective: Critically evaluate the concrete strengths and limitations (and risks) of the IPE server, rather than listing generic advantages.
entries.prompt: Through a step-by-step question-and-answer session, help me identify the concrete strengths of IPE (near-optimal speed close to EDL, low run-time overhead, no wasted CPU time, the Up <= 1 guarantee) and its concrete limitations and risks (high memory for non-harmonic periods, static task set, EDF requirement, complexity, not fully optimal).
entries.ai_output_summary: Claude guided the evaluation one question at a time. I listed the strengths and limitations from my own understanding (built in Milestones 1 and 2), and Claude organized them and added the precise technical wording from Buttazzo, Chapter 6.

actions: Cross-checked the strengths and limitations against the primary reference, Buttazzo, Hard Real-Time Computing Systems, Chapter 6.

issues: The strengths and limitations build on the understanding developed in Milestones 1 and 2; the EDF-requirement limitation was added during the discussion.

integration.section: Section 1 (Concrete Strengths) and Section 2 (Concrete Limitations and Risks)

entries.reflection: The strengths and limitations came from my own understanding of IPE; the AI helped me phrase them as concrete points and added the exact technical terms from the textbook, which I verified.

entries.objective: Identify the hidden or unrealistic assumptions of IPE and analyse its run-time and memory scalability.
entries.prompt: Help me identify which IPE assumptions may be unrealistic in real systems (dynamic task set, multi-core, accurate WCET, full preemption, implicit deadlines) and analyse how IPE's run-time cost and memory cost scale as the system grows.
entries.ai_output_summary: I reasoned that real systems can be dynamic and multi-core, that WCET is hard to know exactly, and that execution times vary; and that IPE's run-time cost stays low (offline work) while its memory cost grows quickly with the hyperperiod. Claude organized these into the assumptions and scalability sections, with details from Buttazzo.

actions: Checked the assumptions and the run-time-versus-memory scalability behaviour against Buttazzo, Chapter 6.

issues: The full-preemption and implicit-deadline assumptions were added from the textbook to complete the list.

integration.section: Section 3 (Hidden or Unrealistic Assumptions) and Section 4 (Scalability Analysis)

entries.reflection: I identified the unrealistic assumptions and the memory-versus-run-time scalability myself; the AI helped me state them clearly and completely using the textbook.

entries.objective: Choose suitable and unsuitable application scenarios for IPE and propose meaningful extensions and open research questions.
entries.prompt: Help me work out a suitable embedded scenario for IPE and an unsuitable one, and propose extensions (reduced-memory IPE, multi-core IPE, adaptive IPE, robust IPE) and open questions.
entries.ai_output_summary: I chose a robot/motor controller as a suitable scenario (fixed harmonic periodic tasks plus soft aperiodic commands) and a fixed-priority AUTOSAR ECU as an unsuitable one, and proposed reduced-memory, multi-core, adaptive, and robust IPE as extensions. Claude organized these and anchored the unsuitable example to a concrete AUTOSAR ECU, with details from the textbook.

actions: Confirmed that AUTOSAR uses fixed-priority scheduling (so IPE cannot run there) and that the suitable-scenario reasoning matches IPE's requirements as described in Buttazzo, Chapter 6.

issues: The application examples were kept general and not tied to a specific commercial product.

integration.section: Section 5 (Suitable Scenario), Section 6 (Unsuitable Scenario), and Section 7 (Extensions and Open Questions)

entries.reflection: I selected the scenarios and the extensions myself, based on IPE's strengths and limitations; the AI helped me express them and add a concrete example for the unsuitable case.
